newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Range bound Australia bonds look to RBA chief.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Range bound Australia bonds look to RBA chief.

text.p: *Australian bond yields ended little changed after a fairly thinly traded, range bound session.
*Focus on RBA's Macfarlane speech to CEDA later today.

Australian bond yields ended little changed with the immediate focus now on a speech by Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane later today, which will set the tone going into the Bank's board meeting next Tuesday.

In particular the market will be interested in his reading of Thursday's latest report on enterprise bargaining agreements given that central bank expressed concerns in its last quarterly Bulletin over their potential threat to wages growth.
Analysts opinions, however, were fairly mixed on the data outcome, although they did show some moderation.
"Today's data was nothing more than a soothing effect to the market place, letting it know that wages aren't out of control," said Frank Sanella, chief analyst at Technical Data.

The Australian Department of Industrial Relations said average annualised wage increases was 4.8 percent for the September quarter, down from a revised 5.3 percent in the previous quarter, while private sector wages rose 5.3 percent from a revised 6.1 percent.
However, other analysts said the private sector outcome was still too high and will keep the central bank cautious about easing monetary policy again.
Macfarlane is due to address the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) at 7.45 p.m. (0845 GMT).

Bond yields dipped initially on the wages report, but were otherwise confined a fairly narrow trading as the market attempted to consolidate after the volatile price action of the past few days, and in the absence of U.S. bond trading in Asia. The U.S. market is closed today for Thanksgiving Day.
Meanwhile, the government was out in force attacking recent Budget blocking revenue measures by Senate minority parties.
Finance minister John Fahey said the blocks could jeopardise the government's plan to balance the budget by 1998/99.
Although of no immediate threat to the bond market, there are potential risks further ahead.

"It's how overseas investors judge the overall policy fix. They had a restrictive budget, but everything since has been a watering back of that," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
"Even though Japanese investors may still be fascinated by the yield differential in 1997, the risk profile is going to be significantly higher," he added.

Yield spreads to other dollar bloc bonds finished wider on the day after a fairly mixed session. The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield margin widened to around 106 basis points initially, but while narrowing on the DIR report, it found resistance in pushing back below 100 basis points.
